# The 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow Disasters: A Definitive Analysis of the Events of June 2–3, 2001
## 1\. Introduction and Historical Significance
The summer of 2001 marked a watershed moment in the history of British civil aviation displays. The Biggin Hill International Air Fair, a venerable institution in the European airshow calendar, became the site of two separate, catastrophic accidents occurring within less than twenty-four hours of one another Hosted at the historic London Biggin Hill Airport—a site synonymous with the Battle of Britain and the defense of London—the 39th annual Air Fair was intended to be a celebration of vintage aviation and military heritage Instead, the weekend of June 2 and 3, 2001, is now remembered as one of the darkest periods in the UK airshow industry, resulting in the deaths of three highly experienced aviators: Air Marshal Sir Kenneth Hayr, Jonathan Kerr, and Guy Bancroft-Wilson .

These disasters involved two distinct types of historic aircraft: a jet-powered de Havilland Vampire T and a piston-engined Bell P-63 Kingcobra While the accident was operationally unrelated—one caused by the invisible aerodynamic hazard of wake turbulence and the other by a loss of control during a vertical maneuver—their temporal proximity created a "nightmare scenario" for airshow organizers and regulators alike The tragedies prompted an immediate suspension of the event, a rigorous investigation by the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB), and a subsequent overhaul of safety protocols governing display flying in the United Kingdom .

This report provides an exhaustive reconstruction of the weekend. It analyzes the operational context, the specific mechanical and human factors contributing to each crash, the findings of the official investigations, and the enduring legacy of these events on the regulation of air displays. By synthesizing data from official reports, witness statements, and technical analyses, this document aims to serve as a comprehensive record of the 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters.

### 1.1 The Venue: Biggin Hill International Air Fair
To understand the magnitude of the 2001 disasters, one must appreciate the stature of the venue. Established in 1963 by Squadron Leader Jock Maitland, the Biggin Hill International Air Fair was the largest privately organized airshow in Europe Maitland, a former RAF Saber pilot and Korean War veteran, had leased the airport from Bromley Council in 1958 and founded the show to support the airport's commercial viability while honoring its wartime legacy .

By 2001, the Air Fair was attracting upward of 35,000 spectators per day It was a premier event that drew participation from major military aerobic teams such as the Red Arrows, as well as a significant gathering of "warbirds"—restored military aircraft from the Second World War and the early Cold War era The airport itself, located on a plateau in Bromley, Kent, presents a challenging but historic stage for display pilots, with its proximity to housing developments and the dense population of Greater London necessitating strict adherence to flight path regulations .

The safety record of the Air Fair prior to 2001 was robust. Organizers frequently defend the safety of the event, noting that the last fatality at a vintage airshow of this scale had occurred decades ago, with some sources citing 1980 as the last comparable incident This perception of safety was shattered over the course of a single weekend, challenging the assumption that the "Zero Error Margin" environment of low-level display flying could be entirely mitigated by regulation and pilot experience .

## 2\. Operational Prelude: Saturday, June 2, 2001
The weekend began with high expectations. The weather conditions were generally favorable for flying, with clear skies and moderate winds, though the specific meteorological conditions would later play a critical role in the analysis of wake turbulence The flying program was ambitious, featuring coordinated displays of multiple vintage aircraft types.

### 2.1 The Precursor Incident: De Havilland Venom (G-GONE)
Before the fatal accident occurred, a serious incident took place on the morning of Saturday, June 2, which set a chaotic tone for the operational schedule and directly affected the circumstances of the first fatal crash.

A de Havilland Venom FB , registered G-GONE and owned by the de Havilland Flying Group, was scheduled to perform as part of a "De Havilland Trio" formation This trio was to consist of the Venom, a de Havilland Vampire, and a de Havilland Sea Vixen—three generations of twin-boom jet fighters designed by the same manufacturer.

During its display routine, the Venom experienced a mechanical failure preventing the deployment of its landing gear. The pilot, Clive Rustin, was forced to execute a belly landing on the runway with the gear retracted Rustin, a former RAF pilot, managed the emergency skillfully; he escaped without injury, and the aircraft suffered only minor structural damage to its fuselage .

Operational Consequences: 
The Venom incident had two critical consequences:

1. **Schedule Disruption:** The runway was closed while cranes were brought in to recover the immobilized aircraft This delay forced a reorganization of the remaining display timetable. 
2. **Formation Modification:** The "De Havilland Trio" was reduced to a pair. The remaining aircraft—the Vampire and the Sea Vixen—were forced to fly a revised "duo" routine. This impromptu change in the display composition will have fatal implications later that afternoon, as the Vampire will now be flying in closer proximity to the much larger Sea Vixen without the spacing typically afforded by a three-ship formation .

## 3\. Disaster I: The De Havilland Vampire Crash (June 2\)
At approximately 18:02 BST, as the day's flying program was nearing its conclusion, the revised de Havilland duo took to the skies The display involved a de Havilland DH . Vampire T flying in formation with a de Havilland Sea Vixen D.3.

### 3.1 Aircraft and Crew Profile
The Aircraft: De Havilland Vampire T (G-DHAV) 
The aircraft involved was a vintage jet trainer, a de Havilland Vampire T with the civil registration G-DHAV .

* **Production History:** Built in 1955 (Construction Number 48913), this airframe was delivered to the Royal Air Force in 1956, serving under the serial XH308. 
* **Swiss Service:** After its RAF service concluded in 1962, it was sold to the Swiss Air Force ( *Flugwaffe* ) in 1967\. In Switzerland, it was upgraded to the Vampire T export standard and operated as U-1234 until 1990\. 
* **Restoration:** The aircraft was repatriated to the UK in 1995 and restored to airworthiness by the de Havilland Flying Group. It was powered by a single Rolls-Royce Goblin Mk 35B turbojet engine .

The Pilot-in-Command: Air Marshal Sir Kenneth Hayr (66) 
The aircraft was flown by one of the most distinguished aviators in the British military establishment.

* **Career:** Sir Kenneth Hayr was a former Deputy Chief of Defense Staff and had served as the Inspector of RAF Flight Safety from 1976 to 1979 He was instrumental in overseeing the RAF's operations during the Falklands War and had commanded No. 1 Squadron (Harriers) in 1969 . 
* **Experience:** He had accumulated a total of 4,398 flying hours, with 185 hours on the Vampire type. His reputation was that of a highly disciplined and safety-conscious pilot, having previously raised concerns about the readiness of Boards of Inquiry to attribute negligence in military accidents .

The Safety Pilot: Jonathan Kerr (33) 
Occupying the right seat was Jonathan Kerr, a passionate vintage aviation enthusiast.

* **Role:** Kerr was assigned as a safety pilot for this specific flight by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) due to the revised nature of the display following the morning's Venom incident . 
* **Background:** Kerr was a commercial pilot and restorer who had recently realized his ambition to acquire and fly his own Vampire. His family later described him as a man who "lived for his passion and died living it" .

### 3.2 The Accident Sequence
The two aircraft, the Vampire and the Sea Vixen, were performing a series of flypasts and maneuvers relative to the crowd line. The Sea Vixen, a powerful twin-engine naval fighter, is significant and generates more thrust than the diminutive Vampire trainer .

The Maneuver: 
The display sequence called for a "wingover"—a maneuver involving a climb and a banked turn to reverse direction. The Sea Vixen led the maneuver, with the Vampire following in close trail . 
The Aerodynamic Upset: 
As the Vampire entered the turn behind the Sea Vixen, it encountered the wake turbulence generated by the leading aircraft.

* **Mechanism:** Wake turbulence consists of counter-rotating vortices shed from an aircraft's wingtips. The strength of these vortices is directly proportional to the weight of the generating aircraft and inversely proportional to its wingspan and speed. The Sea Vixen, being a heavy, swept-wing fighter under G-loading during the turn, was generating powerful vortices . 
* **Loss of Control:** The Vampire hits the Sea Vixen's slipstream and immediately "flicked-in." Witnesses described the aircraft rolling violently and uncontrollably to the right The roll rate induced by the vortex energy exceeds the mechanical authority of the Vampire's ailerons to counter it . 
* **Impact:** The aircraft spiraled downwards, auto-rotating. It struck the ground in a steep nose-down attitude of approximately 45 degrees, banked steeply to the right. The impact occurred about 850 meters from the end of Runway 03/21, in a field near a ridge . 
* **Outcome:** The aircraft disintegrated instantly upon impact, creating a large fireball. Both Sir Kenneth Hayr and Jonathan Kerr were killed immediately. The crash site was approximately 1.5 miles from the main crowd area, ensuring no spectators were injured .

### 3.3 Immediate Aftermath
The crew of the Sea Vixen, realizing the catastrophe occurring behind them, immediately aborted their display. They dumped excess fuel to reduce landing weight and landed safely on Runway 03 The Air Fair was suspended for the remainder of the day as emergency services participated in the scene. The tragic loss of such a high-profile pilot as Sir Kenneth Hayr generated immediate media attention, with reports highlighting the "nightmare scenario" unfolding at Biggin Hill .

## 4\. Disaster II: The Bell P-63 Kingcobra Crash (June 3\)
Despite the tragedy of the previous evening, the decision was made to continue the Air Fair on Sunday, June 3\. The rationale was likely rooted in the tradition of "the show must go on" and the understanding that the Saturday crash was an accident rather than a systemic failure of the event organization However, the tragedy will strike again less than 24 hours later.

### 4.1 Aircraft and Pilot Profile
The Aircraft: Bell P-63A Kingcobra (G-BTWR) 
The second accident involved a rare American fighter aircraft from the Second World War.

* **Identity:** Bell P-63A-7BE Kingcobra, registration G-BTWR (USAAF Serial 42-69097). 
* **History:** Manufactured in 1944, this aircraft was a development of the P-39 Airacobra. It features a unique mid-engine configuration, with the Allison V1710-117 engine mounted behind the pilot, driving the propeller via a long shaft running through the cockpit floor . 
* **Aerodynamics:** The P-63 utilizes a laminar flow wing. While efficient for high-speed flight, laminar flow wings can exhibit abrupt stall characteristics compared to the more forgiving operational envelopes of aircraft like the Spitfire or Mustang. This aerodynamic trait will prove critical in the accident sequence .

The Pilot: Guy Bancroft-Wilson (43) 
The pilot, Guy Bancroft-Wilson, was a consummate professional with a background in elite military and civil aviation.

* **Military Service:** He was a former Royal Air Force pilot who had served with the **Red Arrows** , the world-renowned RAF aerobatic team, for three seasons. Such a posting is reserved for pilots demonstrating exceptional handling skills and discipline . 
* **Civil Career:** At the time of the accident, he was a Captain for British Airways based at Gatwick Airport . 
* **Currency:** He had a total of 7,730 flying hours. However, his experience on the P-63 Kingcobra specifically was limited. Records indicate he had flown only 13 hours on the type. In the 90 days preceding the accident, his practice had included 30 minutes dual in a Harvard and 25 minutes in the Kingcobra on June 1, plus the display on Saturday .

### 4.2 The Accident Sequence
The Kingcobra was part of a scheduled "American Trio" display featuring three US World War II fighters. The group took off and held to the west of the airport for three minutes before commencing their routine .

The Display: 
The three aircraft performed a formation run-in, executing a loop followed by a half Cuban eight. Following this, the Kingcobra broke away from the formation as planned to perform a solo "slot" routine while the other aircraft repositioned . 
The First Incident: 
Approximately one minute into his solo routine, Bancroft-Wilson performed a flypast at 220 knots. He then pulled up into a rolling, climbing maneuver. At the apex of this maneuver, while partially inverted, the aircraft appeared to stall and withdrew controlled flight, entering an incipient spin .

* **Recovery:** Bancroft-Wilson managed to recover the aircraft, but only after losing significant altitude. 
* **Command Failure:** Observing this instability, the Flying Display Committee (FCC)—the safety oversight body for the airshow—issued an instruction for the pilot to land immediately. However, a critical failure occurred in the communications relay between the FCC and Air Traffic Control (ATC). The instructions to "land now" were not transmitted to the pilot in time .

The Fatal Maneuver: 
Unaware of the order to land (or choosing to continue), Bancroft-Wilson resumed his display. He performed a pass from left to right, executed a wingover, and returned for a pass at 190–195 knots He then pulled up into a vertical maneuver, likely intended to be a loop.

* **Energy State:** Analysis of video footage by the AAIB later indicated that the aircraft entered this final maneuver with insufficient speed to complete it safely . 
* **Loss of Control:** At the top of the loop, in an inverted position, the pilot maintains full nose-up elevator and applied a substantial amount of right rudder. These inputs were catastrophic. The AAIB noted that "the flight control inputs... were not consistent with a display maneuver... In fact, they were similar to the control positions used to effect deliberate entry into a spin" . 
* **The Crash:** The aircraft yawed violently to the right and entered an upright incipient spin. With no altitude remaining for recovery, the Kingcobra plummeted towards the ground. 
* **Impact:** The aircraft struck the ground in a steep nose-down attitude to the west of the runway, just 100 yards from the horrified crowd and 200 meters from a housing development The aircraft was destroyed instantly in a fireball, and Guy Bancroft-Wilson was killed .

## 5\. Official Investigations and Findings
The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) launched separate investigations for each fatal crash. These reports, published in 2002, provided detailed forensic and aerodynamic analyzes of the disasters.

### 5.1 Investigation of the Vampire Crash (Report EW/C2001/6/3)
The AAIB investigation into the loss of G-DHAV focused heavily on the phenomenon of wake turbulence.

* **Findings:** The report concludes that the accident was caused by the Vampire entering the wake turbulence of the Sea Vixen. The Sea Vixen, being significantly significant, generated vortices that were calculated to be **quadruple the strength** of those the Vampire itself would generate . 
* **Roll Authority:** The investigation determined that the "equivalent roll acceleration" imposed by the vortex on the Vampire was greater than the maximum roll authority available to the pilot. Even with full opposite aileron, Sir Kenneth Hayr would have been physically unable to stop the uncommanded roll . 
* **Conclusion:** The crash was considered an accident resulting from aerodynamic upset. The proximity of the two aircraft during the maneuver left no margin for error when the trailing aircraft intersected the vortex core .

### 5.2 Investigation of the Kingcobra Crash (Report EW/C2001/6/4)
The investigation into G-BTWR was more complex, involving human factors and aircraft performance limitations.

* **Energy Management:** The primary technical cause was identified as attempting a vertical maneuver with insufficient airspeed . 
* **Pilot Input:** The application of rudder at the apex of the loop was highlighted as a critical error. The inputs were described as inconsistent with recovery and more akin to spin entry inputs. This leads the AAIB to speculate that "an unknown factor affects the pilot's physical and/or mental performance" . 
* **Mentoring:** The report noted a lack of documented mentoring for the pilot on the P-63 type. While he was legally authorized, there was no evidence of specific display evaluation or coaching on the unique handling characteristics of the Kingcobra beyond the basic check flights . 
* **Communication:** The failure of the communications link between the FCC and ATC was noted as a contributing factor, as it prevented the "land now" order from potentially saving the pilot's life after the first error .

## 6\. Inquests and Legal Proceedings
The inquests into the deaths of the three pilots were held at the South London Coroner's Court. The proceedings were emotionally charged, participated by the families of the deceased, including Julian Hayr, the son of Sir Kenneth .

### 6.1 Verdicts
The coroner's jury returned verdicts of **"Accidental Death"** for all three men: Sir Kenneth Hayr, Jonathan Kerr, and Guy Bancroft-Wilson .

* **Implications:** The verdicts confirmed that the deaths were not the result of gross negligence or unfair killing but were tragic consequences of the inherent risks associated with high-performance display flying. 
* **Family Reactions:** The families of Hayr and Kerr display remarkable unity. In a poignant gesture, they agreed to have the two men cremated together, with their ashes scattered at Biggin Hill, symbolizing their shared passion and final moments together Jonathan Kerr's family released a statement eulogizing him as someone who "lived for his passion and died living it" .

## 7\. Regulatory Impact and Legacy
The 2001 Biggin Hill disasters had a profound and lasting impact on the regulation of airshows in the United Kingdom. The proximity of the crashes to residential areas and the loss of such high-profile pilots forced the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to review its guidance comprehensively.

### 7.1 Revisions to CAP 403
**CAP 403** , the CAA's document titled "Flying Displays and Special Events: A Guide to Safety and Administrative Arrangements," underwent significant revision after the accident .

* **Flying Control Committees (FCC):** The role of the FCC was strengthened. Post-2001 guidance clarified that FCCs must have a member positioned on the crowd line with direct, fail-safe communication to the Flying Display Director (FDD) to ensure that any "stop" or "land" calls are immediately relayed to pilots This directly addressed the communication failure noted in the Kingcobra investigation. 
* **Mentoring and Evaluation:** The investigation into Bancroft-Wilson's crash highlights the need for rigorous mentoring. New requirements emphasize that pilots transitioning to complex vintage types must undergo specific display evaluations and mentoring, rather than relying solely on general display authorizations . 
* **Wake Turbulence Separation:** The Vampire crash led to stricter guidelines regarding formation flying between dissimilar aircraft types. Briefings now strongly emphasize the required separation distances and flight path offsets to avoid wake encounters, particularly when jets of greatly different weights are maneuvering together .

### 7.2 The End of an Era
While the Biggin Hill Air Fair returned in 2002 and continued for several years, the "nightmare scenario" of 2001 hung over the event. The increased insurance costs and the scrutiny on safety changed the atmosphere of the show .

In 2010, Biggin Hill Airport Ltd canceled the contract with Air Displays International, the organizers of the Air Fair, ending a 47-year tradition The airport management cited a strategic shift towards business aviation. However, the legacy of the 2001 disasters—and the subsequent tightening of regulations—undoubtedly played a role in the diminishing viability of such a massive vintage airshow at that specific location .

### 7.3 The Festival of Flight
In 2014, airshows returned to Biggin Hill in the form of the **Festival of Flight** .3This new event was markedly different from the old Air Fair. It was smaller, with a capped attendance of 18,000, and focused heavily on community relations and safety Under the directorship of Will Curtis, the Festival implements the lessons learned since 2001, operating under the stricter modern regulatory framework to ensure the safety of both the pilots and the surrounding population of Bromley .

## 8\. Technical Data Summary
The following table presents a comparative summary of the technical data for the two accidents:

| Feature | Disaster I (June 2, 2001\) | Disaster II (June 3, 2001\) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Aircraft Type** | De Havilland DH . Vampire T | Bell P-63A-7BE Kingcobra |
| **Registration** | G-DHAV (ex-RAF XH308) | G-BTWR (ex-USAAF 42-69097) |
| **Engine** | Rolls-Royce Goblin Mk 35B Turbojet | Allison V1710-117 Piston |
| **Pilot(s)** | Sir Kenneth Hayr (66), Jonathan Kerr (33) | Guy Bancroft-Wilson (43) |
| **Fatalities** | 2 | 1 |
| **Time of Accident** | 18:02 BST | 15:44 BST |
| **the Cause** | Aerodynamic Upset (Wake Turbulence) | Loss of Control (Stall/Spin) |
| **Key Factor** | Sea Vixen wingtip vortices | Insufficient energy; Rudder input |
| **Impact Location** | 850m from Runway 03/21 | West of runway, near housing |
| **AAIB Report Ref** | EW/C2001/6/3 | EW/C2001/6/4 |

## 9\. Conclusion
The 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters serve as a somber reminder of the unforgiving nature of aviation. The weekend began with a celebration of the "De Havilland Trio" and the "American Warbirds" but ended in the loss of three lives and two historic airframes.

The investigation into the Vampire crash illuminates the lethal power of wake turbulence, invisible yet capable of overpowering a pilot as experienced as Sir Kenneth Hayr. The Kingcobra crash highlights the critical importance of energy management and the potential for human error even among the most elite pilots, such as former Red Arrows members.

Finally, the legacy of June 2001 is found in the enhanced safety protocols that govern UK airshows today. The revisions to CAP 403, the empowerment of Flying Control Committees, and the stricter mentoring requirements are the direct result of the lessons learned from the tragedies of G-DHAV and G-BTWR. These changes ensure that while the spectacle of flight continues to inspire, the "Zero Error Margin" is managed with the utmost rigor to protect those in the air and on the ground.

Approximately one minute into his solo routine, Bancroft-Wilson performed a flypast at 220 knots.
Bancroft-Wilson then pulled up into a rolling, climbing maneuver.
At the apex of this maneuver, while partially inverted, the aircraft appeared to stall and withdrew controlled flight, entering an incipient spin.
Bancroft-Wilson managed to recover the aircraft, but only after losing significant altitude.
Observing this instability, the Flying Display Committee (FCC)—the safety oversight body for the airshow—issued an instruction for the pilot to land immediately.
However, a critical failure occurred in the communications relay between the FCC and Air Traffic Control (ATC).
The instructions to "land now" were not transmitted to the pilot in time.
Unaware of the order to land (or choosing to continue), Bancroft-Wilson resumed his display.
Bancroft-Wilson performed a pass from left to right, executed a wingover, and returned for a pass at 190–195 knots.
Bancroft-Wilson then pulled up into a vertical maneuver, likely intended to be a loop.
Analysis of video footage by the AAIB later indicated that the aircraft entered this final maneuver with insufficient speed to complete it safely.
At the top of the loop, in an inverted position, the pilot maintains full nose-up elevator and applied a substantial amount of right rudder.
These inputs were catastrophic.
The AAIB noted that "the flight control inputs... were not consistent with a display maneuver... In fact, they were similar to the control positions used to effect deliberate entry into a spin".
The aircraft yawed violently to the right and entered an upright incipient spin.
With no altitude remaining for recovery, the Kingcobra plummeted towards the ground.
The aircraft struck the ground in a steep nose-down attitude to the west of the runway, just 100 yards from the horrified crowd and 200 meters from a housing development.
The aircraft was destroyed instantly in a fireball, and Guy Bancroft-Wilson was killed.
The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) launched separate investigations for each fatal crash.
These reports, published in 2002, provided detailed forensic and aerodynamic analyzes of the disasters.
The AAIB investigation into the loss of G-DHAV focused heavily on the phenomenon of wake turbulence.
The report concludes that the accident was caused by the Vampire entering the wake turbulence of the Sea Vixen.
The Sea Vixen, being significantly significant, generated vortices that were calculated to be quadruple the strength of those the Vampire itself would generate.
The investigation determined that the "equivalent roll acceleration" imposed by the vortex on the Vampire was greater than the maximum roll authority available to the pilot.
Even with full opposite aileron, Sir Kenneth Hayr would have been physically unable to stop the uncommanded roll.
The crash was considered an accident resulting from aerodynamic upset.
The proximity of the two aircraft during the maneuver left no margin for error when the trailing aircraft intersected the vortex core.
The investigation into G-BTWR was more complex, involving human factors and aircraft performance limitations.
The primary technical cause was identified as attempting a vertical maneuver with insufficient airspeed.
The application of rudder at the apex of the loop was highlighted as a critical error.
The inputs were described as inconsistent with recovery and more akin to spin entry inputs.
This leads the AAIB to speculate that "an unknown factor affects the pilot's physical and/or mental performance".
The report noted a lack of documented mentoring for the pilot on the P-63 type.
While the pilot was legally authorized, there was no evidence of specific display evaluation or coaching on the unique handling characteristics of the Kingcobra beyond the basic check flights.
The failure of the communications link between the FCC and ATC was noted as a contributing factor, as it prevented the "land now" order from potentially saving the pilot's life after the first error.
The inquests into the deaths of the three pilots were held at the South London Coroner's Court.
The proceedings were emotionally charged, participated by the families of the deceased, including Julian Hayr, the son of Sir Kenneth.
The coroner's jury returned verdicts of "Accidental Death" for all three men: Sir Kenneth Hayr, Jonathan Kerr, and Guy Bancroft-Wilson.
The verdicts confirmed that the deaths were not the result of gross negligence or unfair killing but were tragic consequences of the inherent risks associated with high-performance display flying.
The families of Hayr and Kerr displayed remarkable unity.

In a poignant gesture, the families of Hayr and Kerr agreed to have the two men cremated together, with their ashes scattered at Biggin Hill, symbolizing their shared passion and final moments together.
Jonathan Kerr's family released a statement eulogizing him as someone who "lived for his passion and died living it".
The 2001 Biggin Hill disasters had a profound and lasting impact on the regulation of airshows in the United Kingdom.
The proximity of the crashes to residential areas and the loss of such high-profile pilots forced the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to review its guidance comprehensively.
CAP 403, the CAA's document titled "Flying Displays and Special Events: A Guide to Safety and Administrative Arrangements," underwent significant revision after the accident.
The role of the FCC (Flying Control Committees) was strengthened.

Post-2001 guidance clarified that FCCs must have a member positioned on the crowd line with direct, fail-safe communication to the Flying Display Director (FDD) to ensure that any "stop" or "land" calls are immediately relayed to pilots.
This directly addressed the communication failure noted in the Kingcobra investigation.
The investigation into Bancroft-Wilson's crash highlights the need for rigorous mentoring.
New requirements emphasize that pilots transitioning to complex vintage types must undergo specific display evaluations and mentoring, rather than relying solely on general display authorizations.
The Vampire crash led to stricter guidelines regarding formation flying between dissimilar aircraft types.
Briefings now strongly emphasize the required separation distances and flight path offsets to avoid wake encounters, particularly when jets of greatly different weights are maneuvering together.
While the Biggin Hill Air Fair returned in 2002 and continued for several years, the "nightmare scenario" of 2001 hung over the event.
The increased insurance costs and the scrutiny on safety changed the atmosphere of the show.
In 2010, Biggin Hill Airport Ltd canceled the contract with Air Displays International, the organizers of the Air Fair, ending a 47-year tradition.
The airport management cited a strategic shift towards business aviation.

However, the legacy of the 2001 disasters—and the subsequent tightening of regulations—undoubtedly played a role in the diminishing viability of such a massive vintage airshow at that specific location.
In 2014, airshows returned to Biggin Hill in the form of the Festival of Flight.
This new event was markedly different from the old Air Fair.
The Festival of Flight was smaller, with a capped attendance of 18,000, and focused heavily on community relations and safety.

Under the directorship of Will Curtis, the Festival implements the lessons learned since 2001, operating under the stricter modern regulatory framework to ensure the safety of both the pilots and the surrounding population of Bromley.
The 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters serve as a somber reminder of the unforgiving nature of aviation.
The weekend began with a celebration of the "De Havilland Trio" and the "American Warbirds" but ended in the loss of three lives and two historic airframes.
The investigation into the Vampire crash illuminates the lethal power of wake turbulence, invisible yet capable of overpowering a pilot as experienced as Sir Kenneth Hayr.
The Kingcobra crash highlights the critical importance of energy management and the potential for human error even among the most elite pilots, such as former Red Arrows members.
Finally, the legacy of June 2001 is found in the enhanced safety protocols that govern UK airshows today.
The revisions to CAP 403, the empowerment of Flying Control Committees, and the stricter mentoring requirements are the direct result of the lessons learned from the tragedies of G-DHAV and G-BTWR.
These changes ensure that while the spectacle of flight continues to inspire, the "Zero Error Margin" is managed with the utmost rigor to protect those in the air and on the ground.

The **Biggin Hill International Air Show**, or **Biggin Hill Air Fair**, was one of the largest civilian airshows in the world and the largest privately organised air show in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"). It ran once a year, usually near the end of June, at [London Biggin Hill Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport "London Biggin Hill Airport"), a former [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") RAF fighter station, from 1963 to 2010. It has been succeeded by a smaller-scale air show event titled _The Festival of Flight_ which was launched in June 2014.

History
-------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[Squadron Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squadron_Leader "Squadron Leader") Jock Maitland purchased a lease to run [Biggin Hill Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_Airport "Biggin Hill Airport") from [Bromley Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Bromley "London Borough of Bromley") in 1958, and commenced the first show in 1963. Jock Maitland had flown Sabres in conflict in Korea before retiring from RAF service. He started a small charter company, Maitland Air Charter which operated pleasure flights from Ramsgate Airport during 1959 and 1960, eventually using former RAF [Percival Prentice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percival_Prentice "Percival Prentice") aircraft refurbished and civilianised by Aviation Traders of Southend, a company started by [Freddie Laker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Laker "Freddie Laker"). Subsequently, Jock set up in business with a local builder to form Maitland Drewery Aviation and operated Vickers Viscount aircraft. Drewery conceived the infamous steel Wendy House which once graced the Apron on Biggin Hill Airport. The council privatised the airport in 1988 and it was bought by Biggin Hill Airport Ltd in 1994, who agreed a 25-year contract for the air fair.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair#cite_note-Nelson-1)

In 2010 Biggin Hill Airport Ltd, the airfield leaseholders, cancelled the licence to run the air fair after 47 years, three years before it was due to end.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair#cite_note-Nelson-1)

On Saturday 14 June 2014, the air fair was revived with a new smaller-scale format entitled _The Festival of Flight_. The proposed annual one-day event was limited to 15,000 spectators and was meant to portray Biggin Hill as both a site of historical value and as a modern thriving business airport. The main attraction of the show was a display from the [Red Arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Arrows "Red Arrows") who were celebrating their 50th Display year - Biggin Hill was notable for being the site of the first public display for the aerobatic display team in the UK back in 1965. A second Festival of Flight took place in June 2015, with a third held in June 2016.

From 2017 (the 100th anniversary of the [RFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Flying_Corps "Royal Flying Corps") starting to use the airfield), the event took place over 2 days in August.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair#cite_note-2)

In 2020, instead of a Festival of Flight (which could not have been held owing to significant infrastructure projects taking place at the airport), it was planned that a public event would be held on 10 August entitled "[The Hardest Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hardest_Day "The Hardest Day")", to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the [Battle of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair#cite_note-3) However, owing to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), this event was cancelled.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair#cite_note-4)

Airfair Radio
-------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Airfair Radio")]

Airfair Radio was a Restricted Service Broadcaster [radio station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_station "Radio station") which covered the Air Fair from 1989 until 2006. It broadcast locally for between three and seven days each year on the [FM band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FM_band "FM band") and worldwide via the [internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_radio "Internet radio"). Airfair Radio broadcast live from the [airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airfield "Airfield") 24 hours of the day, with programmes of commentary, [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music"), [interviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interview "Interview"), [phone-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phone-in "Phone-in") competitions, local current affairs and dedications. Some of the calls received were relayed over the airwaves via phone–in equipment. Calls to the studio often numbered in excess of 200 a day.

Running a radio station from the middle of an airfield posed some unusual challenges. Electrical power came from a [generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_generator "Electrical generator"), accommodation was expensive and costs were high for a temporary telephone line. The station was paid for by spot advertising and [sponsorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponsorship "Sponsorship").

Airfair Radio first began broadcasting in 1989 on FM. For many years it broadcast on [AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AM_radio "AM radio"); however, for the last six years of transmission from Biggin Hill, FM was the preferred method of delivery. The broadcasts were simulcast over the internet, allowing programmes to be heard worldwide.

The station was operated by volunteers, many of whom worked in the broadcasting and communications industries; this allowed it to draw on a variety of experience from associated fields.

Its commentators were pilots, with many years of experience under their belts; the station's senior commentator, Ian Marshall, was a [Sony Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Award "Sony Award")-winning broadcaster.[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] Many of its presenters and producers have gone on to develop successful broadcasting careers. Among them: Sam Matterface, who worked at the south-coast radio station 107.4 The Quay, where he presented the breakfast show and a variety of sports related programmes from 2001 to 2007, then moving on to presenting on Sky Sports News in July 2007, before leaving in late 2010. He is now the chief football commentator for TalkSport, and ITV Sport, and is the commentator for ITV's Dancing on Ice; Harvey Cook, News reader and writer, continuity announcer for BBC Radio 5Live, 6Music and Radio 2; Paul Stafford, who has a daily radio programme in Australia, and Fiona Goldman, whose credits include radio presenter for the British Forces Broadcasting Services, features reporter for BBC Radio 4, newsreader for BBC World Service and announcer for ITV and SKY. She is also a voice actress for TV and radio commercials and works internationally as a narrator for corporate films, books and documentaries. Other members of the team have pursued careers as producers for both BBC and Independent Radio stations, and in broadcast television.

Although AirFair Radio first started broadcasting in 1989, its volunteer team had been involved in local broadcasting for many years previously. Under the banner of SouthEast Radio, the group organised local RSL stations for a number of organisations, including: RoundTable Radio for Farnborough Round Table and Petts Wood Round Table, and Bromley Carnival Radio for The Bromley Carnival Association. Their first venture into local broadcasting was for coverage of the Orpington Town Carnival in 1984.

The establishment of the Special Events Group was born of a need to raise money in support of Orpington Hospital Radio Service, which had been providing programmes for [Orpington Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpington_Hospital "Orpington Hospital") since 1980, and later also for Farnborough hospital. It also provided opportunities for many keen volunteers to acquire skills useful for pursuing careers as producers, presenters, voice-over artists and engineers which, as mentioned above, served many of them well in helping them establish careers in broadcasting.

**London Biggin Hill Airport** (IATA: **BQH**,ICAO: **EGKB**) is an operational general aviation airport at Biggin Hill in the London Borough of Bromley, located 12 NM (22 km; 14 mi) south-southeast of Central London. The airport was formerly the [Royal Air Force](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") station **RAF Biggin Hill**, and a small enclave on the airport still retains that designation.

Biggin Hill is best known for its role during the [Battle of Britain](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain") in the [Second World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), when it served as one of the principal [fighter](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Fighter_aircraft "Fighter aircraft") bases protecting London and South East England from attack by enemy [bombers](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Bomber "Bomber"). Over the course of the war, fighters based at Biggin Hill claimed 1,400 enemy aircraft, at the cost of the lives of 453 Biggin Hill based aircrew.[[3]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhbattle-3)[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-ehbh-4)

Today the airport has a CAA Ordinary Licence (Number P804) that allows flights for the public transport of passengers or for flying instruction as authorised by the licensee (Regional Airports Limited). It specialises in general aviation, handling a spectrum of traffic from private aviation to large business jets. It currently has no scheduled airline service.[[5]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhhome-5)[[6]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-caaol-6)

History of the airport[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FLondon_Biggin_Hill_Airport%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The airfield was originally opened by the [Royal Flying Corps](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Royal_Flying_Corps "Royal Flying Corps") (RFC) during the [First World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). At first it was used for wireless experiments, but was then established in 1917 as part of the London Air Defence Area, responsible for defending the capital against attacks by [Zeppelins](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Zeppelin "Zeppelin") and [Gotha bombers](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Gotha_bomber "Gotha bomber"). To this end, 141 Squadron of the RFC was based at Biggin Hill and equipped with [Bristol Fighters](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Bristol_F.2_Fighter "Bristol F.2 Fighter").[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhphist-7)

Between the wars, the airfield was used by a number of experimental units, working on instrument design, ground based anti-aircraft defences, and night flying. The base was closed between 1929 and 1932, during which period reconstruction work took place including the building of new hangars.[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhphist-7)

During the Second World War the airfield was one of the commanding bases for the [Battle of Britain](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain"), with both [Spitfires](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Supermarine_Spitfire "Supermarine Spitfire") and [Hurricanes](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Hawker_Hurricane "Hawker Hurricane") from a variety of squadrons being based there. The squadrons based at Biggin Hill claimed to have destroyed 1,400 enemy aircraft, at the cost of the lives of 453 Biggin Hill based aircrew. Because of its importance to the capital's defence, the airport itself became a target. Between August 1940 and January 1941, the airfield was attacked twelve times, the worst of which wrecked workshops, stores, barracks, [WAAF](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Women%27s_Auxiliary_Air_Force "Women's Auxiliary Air Force") quarters and a hangar, killing 39 people on the ground.[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-ehbh-4)[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhphist-7)

After the war, Biggin Hill was briefly used by the RAF's Transport Command, and then became a base for both regular and reserve fighter squadrons, flying Spitfires, [Meteors](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Gloster_Meteor "Gloster Meteor") and [Hunters](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Hawker_Hunter "Hawker Hunter"). An infamous day in 1951 (see incidents and accidents below) caused the station's continued use by the military to be called into question. However in 1958 Biggin Hill ceased to be an operational RAF station, becoming the Officer and Aircrew Selection Centre for the RAF. Due to the impending closure of the nearby original London Airport at Croydon, from 1956 much of the civilian light aviation from Croydon relocated to Biggin and it became a joint civilian and military airport. Croydon closed completely in 1959, at which time Biggin Hill became a mainly civilian airport with only occasional military flying taking place.[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhphist-7)

Towards the end of 1963, the Orpington Urban District Council (within whose boundaries the airfield lay) was approached by the Board of Trade as to whether the Council would purchase (effectively from the RAF) Biggin Hill airfield. In 1964, on formation of the London Borough of Bromley, which absorbed Orpington, the offer to purchase was open to the new borough. Protracted negotiations were held with the Board of Trade and later the Department of Trade and Industry. At a special meeting on 15 June 1972 the Council decided to purchase the airport by a recorded vote of 41 to 9. The purchase was eventually completed in 1974.

In May 1992 the Department of Transport issued a direction to the Council under s.13 of the Airports Act 1986. The effect of this direction, which affected airports generating turnover of £1million or more (Biggin Hill just scraped into this limit), was to require the Council to set up a new company for the purpose of operating the airport as an independent commercial undertaking. To comply with the direction would have required the transfer of all the assets and liabilities to the company with a consequential loss of Council control over airport activities. In the circumstances, the Council decided that the granting of a 125 year lease would enable more control to be retained than an outright disposal of the freehold or by a transfer to a local authority company with an uncertain future. In May 1994, the airport was leased to Biggin Hill Airport Limited ("BHAL") for 125 years.[[8]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhfhist-8) BHAL is a subsidiary of Regional Airports Ltd.

Meanwhile, the Officer and Aircrew Selection Centre moved to [RAF Cranwell](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/RAF_Cranwell "RAF Cranwell") in 1992, marking the end of active RAF involvement.[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhphist-7)

In 2001, the London Borough of Bromley as freeholder of the airport succeeded in an action in the Court of Appeal. The court ruling prohibits the airport operators from allowing tickets to be sold for flights into and out of the airport, thus preventing its use for scheduled or holiday charter flights, but allowing business aviation and corporate shuttles.[[9]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhpass-9)

The airport is located on a hill top, just to the east of the Bromley to Westerham road (A233) and about 1 mile (1.6 km) to the north of the town of Biggin Hill. The small village of Leaves Green lies adjacent to the north-western perimeter of the airport.[[10]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-osexp1-10)

The airport has two runways, aligned roughly north-south and east-west, which intersect at their respective southern and western ends, forming an L shaped configuration. The longer north-south oriented runway (03/21) is 1,820 metres in length, making it usable by aircraft up to Boeing 737/Airbus A320 size, and it has an [Instrument Landing System](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Instrument_Landing_System "Instrument Landing System"). Radar air traffic control (ATC) services are provided by Thames Radar at the London Terminal Control Centre, while procedural approach and VFR ATC services are provided by the airport itself.[[11]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhplan-11)[[12]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhmax-12)[[13]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhashm-13)

Despite the effective ban on scheduled services, Biggin Hill is used by a large number of business flights by business jets and similar sized aircraft. The airport has a passenger terminal, located on the A233 road just south of Leaves Green, which provides facilities for such flights, including departure lounges, a licensed café bar, and customs and immigration facilities.[[13]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhashm-13)

The current RAF Biggin Hill is a small enclave on the western boundary of the airport to the south of the passenger terminal, and contains the headquarters of 2427 Squadron of the [Air Training Corps](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Air_Training_Corps "Air Training Corps"). Next to this is St George's Chapel of Remembrance. This brick built chapel was erected in 1951, to replace an earlier chapel destroyed by fire, and now serves as a memorial to all the aircrew who died flying from the Biggin Hill Sector. It is surrounded by a garden of remembrance and has [gate guardians](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Gate_guardian "Gate guardian") in the form of full-sized replicas of a Hurricane and a Spitfire, representing the aircraft that flew from the former airfield during the Battle of Britain. The replicas replaced genuine aircraft that formerly served as the guardians.[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhphist-7)[[14]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-atc2427-14)[[15]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-bhchapel-15)

Besides the passenger terminal and RAF enclave, other former RAF buildings still exist in the 'North Camp' to the west of the main runway, including the Sergeant's Mess of 1932, the Airmen's Institute of circa 1926, the former Station Headquarters building of 1931 and several [barrack](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Barracks "Barracks") blocks. The buildings, which are Grade II listed, are in a redbrick neo-Georgian style typical of military airfields of the inter-war period. They have been vacant since the Officer and Aircrew Selection Centre closed in 1992, and were added to English Heritage's list of buildings at risk in 2006.[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-ehbh-4)

The 'South Camp', situated to the south of runway 11/29, was transferred to civil usage in the 1950s and now consists of a utilitarian collection of hangars and sheds, together with a modern office park. It now contains many aviation related businesses, flying clubs and flying schools. Many private light aircraft are based on the airport.

From 1963, Biggin Hill airport was the venue of the Biggin Hill International Air Fair, an annual airshow that usually took place towards the end of June. On 5 July 2010 Biggin Hill Airport Ltd cancelled the 25 year contract with Air Displays International (the Air Fair organisers) without warning, a few weeks after the 2010 event, during which the Air Fair had attracted record breaking crowds.[Air Displays International](http://www.synergyeventsuk.com/biggin-hill-air-fair/future-air-fair-management-reflects-modern-circumstances)

Construction on a new state-of-the-art hangar alongside the Passenger Terminal commenced in October 2010. Excavations of the site uncovered underground war-time fuel tanks and associated pump rooms; these were re-covered during the same building works. Construction was planned to finish late in Spring 2011.

Biggin Hill is the location of one of the four "stacks" for aircraft landing at Heathrow Airport, and is used by aircraft approaching from the south east. It uses a VOR navigational beacon with the identifier "BIG". Noise from aircraft using this stack is often wrongly attributed to aircraft using Biggin Hill Airport.

Three model aircraft clubs operate within a three mile radius of Biggin Hill Airport. One site operates within its Aerodrome Traffic Zone (2.5 NM (4.6 km; 2.9 mi) radius)[[16]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-16)

In the grounds of the airport an Air Scout centre can be found. The centre allows young people aged between 7 and 18 to take part in aviation activities with their scout groups.

The Airfield still retains its history by the continued restoration projects running at the Biggin Hill Heritage Hangar. IntotheBlue experience days, a UK company within the airfield allows members of the public to fly alongside a Mk9 Spitfire in a 1950's Harvard. It's projects like this, which hold a timely reminder to how important the airport was during the First World War.

No commercial airlines fly to Biggin Hill, as aircraft flying there are not permitted to carry fare-paying passengers.[[17]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-newsshopper-17) An application by the airport to allow such flights around the time of the 2012 London Olympics was rejected by Bromley Council in March 2011.[[17]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-newsshopper-17)

Accidents[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FLondon_Biggin_Hill_Airport%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

*   On 18 June 1951, three Meteors crashed and their pilots were killed in accidents, all three crashing in an area of about 100 yd (91 m). The first, a Meteor VIII piloted by Flight Lieutenant Gordon McDonald of 41 Squadron, crashed shortly after take-off, corkscrewing as pieces of structure fell from the aircraft. The aircraft hit a bungalow, killing the pilot. The jet wash of his flight leader was named as a possible cause. Within seconds of this accident two Mark IV Meteors of 600 Sqn, piloted by Sergeant Kenneth Clarkson and Squadron Leader Phillip Sandeman, both circling over the wreckage and preparing to land, collided at 2,000 ft (610 m) above the scene. Although Sandeman managed to bail out, he was killed when his parachute failed to open. Clarkson was killed in his aircraft. A week after this incident, another Meteor overshot the runway, narrowly missing passing cars. After these incidents, several residents stated they would be "selling up" and there were calls for traffic lights to be installed on the Bromley road for use during take-offs and landings.[[18]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-18)

*   On 15 May 1977, during the annual International Air Fair, a Bell 206 was in a mid-air collision with a [de Havilland Tiger Moth](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/De_Havilland_Tiger_Moth "De Havilland Tiger Moth") at the airport. The Tiger Moth landed but the Bell 206 crashed, killing all five on board.[[19]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-19)

*   On 21 September 1980 a [Douglas B-26 Invader](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Douglas_B-26_Invader "Douglas B-26 Invader") (registered N3710G) crashed during an air display. The aircraft was attempting to carry out a climbing roll in front of the crowd when the nose dropped sharply, and the aircraft continued rolling until it dropped vertically into a valley. The pilot and seven passengers were killed. The Civil Aviation Authority subsequently introduced rules preventing passengers from being carried during air displays.[[20]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-20)

*   On 2 June 2001 a vintage [de Havilland Vampire](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire") jet crashed during an air display, killing both pilots. The Vampire had been flying a display in tandem with a [de Havilland Sea Vixen](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/De_Havilland_Sea_Vixen "De Havilland Sea Vixen") aircraft, and the likely cause of the accident was that the Vampire's flight path had been disrupted by wake turbulence from the larger aircraft.[[21]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-21)

*   On 3 June 2001 a 1944 [Bell P-63 Kingcobra](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Bell_P-63_Kingcobra "Bell P-63 Kingcobra") crashed during a display, killing the pilot. The American Second World War fighter aircraft had been flying an unplanned sequence, when the pilot lost control at the top of a climbing manoeuvre and was unable to recover from the resulting dive. The aircraft impacted the ground to the west of the runway in a steep nose-down attitude.[[22]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-22)

*   On 22 October 2005 a two-seat Piper Tomahawk aircraft on a training flight crashed shortly after take-off from Biggin Hill, killing the flight instructor and his student. The aircraft came down in a residential street, Victoria Gardens, but there were no casualties on the ground. The cause of the accident was found to be a worn fuel filler cap that had allowed water to seep into the fuel tank.[[23]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-23)

*   On 30 March 2008 a Cessna Citation 501 aircraft crashed into a housing estate north of the airfield, killing all five people on board. Shortly after take-off from Biggin Hill, the pilot had reported severe engine vibration and was attempting to return to the airfield when the aircraft crashed. An investigation concluded that both engines had been shut down (possibly inadvertently) during the course of the short flight. Among those killed were Eurosport commentator and former Touring Car driver David Leslie and ex-Le Mans driver Richard Lloyd.[[24]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport#cite_note-BBC-24)

2.title: 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters
2.content:
2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters[![Image 1: Large explosion occurs near a brick building, smoke and flames rising into the sky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b5/Kingcobra_biggin_hill_airshow.jpg/250px-Kingcobra_biggin_hill_airshow.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kingcobra_biggin_hill_airshow.jpg)
Immediate aftermath of the Kingcobra aircraft crash on June 3, 2001.
Disasters
Date June 2, 2001 (Venom/Vampire)

June 3, 2001 (Kingcobra)
Summary Individual accidents
Site[London Biggin Hill Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport "London Biggin Hill Airport"), Bromley, England. 

![Image 2: Show location on an interactive map](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/WMA_button2b.png/20px-WMA_button2b.png)[51°19′51″N 0°1′57″E / 51.33083°N 0.03250°E](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters&params=51_19_51_N_0_1_57_E_type:event)
[![Image 3: Map](https://maps.wikimedia.org/img/osm-intl,7,51.330833333333,0.0325,270x200.png?lang=en&domain=en.wikipedia.org&title=2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters&revid=1328077491&groups=_dba023d9fd5f2aaefa4345809db8c9340c80a657&parser=legacy) [Wikimedia](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Maps_Terms_of_Use) | © [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#/map/0 "Show in full screen")
Total fatalities 3
First aircraft
Type[de Havilland Venom-FB.50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Venom "De Havilland Venom")
Operator[de Havilland Flying Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Havilland_Flying_Group&action=edit&redlink=1 "De Havilland Flying Group (page does not exist)")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKVAMP-1)
[Registration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_registration "Aircraft registration")G-GONE
Crew Clive Rustin (survived)
Second aircraft
Type[de Havilland DH.115 Vampire T Mk 55](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire")
Operator[de Havilland Flying Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Havilland_Flying_Group&action=edit&redlink=1 "De Havilland Flying Group (page does not exist)")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-ASNVAMP-2)
Registration G-DHAV (XH308 and U-1234[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKVAMP-1))
Crew[Kenneth Hayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Hayr "Kenneth Hayr")(killed)

Jonathan Kerr (killed)
Third aircraft
Type[Bell P-63A-7BE Kingcobra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_P-63_Kingcobra "Bell P-63 Kingcobra")
Operator[Patina Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patina_Ltd&action=edit&redlink=1 "Patina Ltd (page does not exist)")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-ASNKC-3)
Registration G-BTWR (42-69097 and N52113[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-AVADKC-4))
Crew Guy Bancroft-Wilson (killed)

Two [aviation disasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_disaster "Aviation disaster") occurred on June 2–3, 2001, during the annual [Biggin Hill Airshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair "Biggin Hill International Air Fair"),[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-5) at [London Biggin Hill Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Biggin_Hill_Airport "London Biggin Hill Airport") in [Bromley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromley "Bromley"), England. An aircraft landing incident and two separate fatal aircraft crashes occurred during the weekend show. A [de Havilland Venom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Venom "De Havilland Venom") suffered minor damage to its [fuselage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuselage "Fuselage") when it landed with its [landing gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_gear "Landing gear") retracted. Six hours later, a [de Havilland DH-115 Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire") was attempting a [wingover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wingover "Wingover"), when the aircraft [lost control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loss_of_control_(aeronautics) "Loss of control (aeronautics)") and dived into the ground, destroying the Vampire and killing pilots [Kenneth Hayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Hayr "Kenneth Hayr") and Jonathan Kerr. A [Bell P-63 Kingcobra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_P-63_Kingcobra "Bell P-63 Kingcobra") crashed the following day after attempting a [maneuver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerobatic_maneuver "Aerobatic maneuver") with insufficient speed, destroying the aircraft and killing pilot Guy Bancroft-Wilson.

After the conclusion of the airshow, the [Air Accidents Investigation Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Accidents_Investigation_Branch "Air Accidents Investigation Branch") opened three investigations into the events of June 2–3 for the Venom, Vampire and Kingcobra respectively. Their findings on how [wake turbulence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_turbulence "Wake turbulence") affects aircraft during [air displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_display "Air display") and how communication issues could be improved between performing aircraft and [air traffic control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_control "Air traffic control") were published in their individual reports. The residents of [Biggin Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill "Biggin Hill") agreed that the weekend had been a terrible tragedy and were divided over whether the airshow should continue. Despite the concern, the airshow continued to run annually until 2011, at which time it was replaced by an open house air day.

### Biggin Hill Airshow

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Biggin Hill Airshow")]

The Biggin Hill Airshow, then known simply as the [Air Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_International_Air_Fair "Biggin Hill International Air Fair"), was first held in 1963 by World War II [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") pilot Jock Maitland.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-TS2012-6) These displays took place at [Biggin Hill Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biggin_Hill_Airport "Biggin Hill Airport") annually for the public to view, with the 25th anniversary held in 1987, by which time the [air show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_show "Air show") had become renowned for having high standards for entertainment and well regarded commentators Roger Hoefling and John Blake.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-RFADI88-7) Early Air Fairs included air displays with the [T-28D Trojan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_T-28_Trojan "North American T-28 Trojan") in 1978 and the [English Electric Lightning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric_Lightning "English Electric Lightning") in 1980.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GARPF-8)

### de Havilland DH-115 Vampire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: de Havilland DH-115 Vampire")]

The DH115 Vampire T11 used in the June 2 display was originally built in 1955 by [de Havilland Aircraft Company Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland "De Havilland") and entered the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") in 1956 under the [registration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_registration "Aircraft registration") of XH308. It remained in service until 1962, after which the aircraft was put into storage, sold to the [Swiss Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_Air_Force "Swiss Air Force") and was then upgraded to Mk 55.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-F9DBA-9) The Vampire operated as U-1234 through 1991, finally being returned to the United Kingdom in 1995.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKVAMP-1)

Piloting the Vampire was [Sir Kenneth Hayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Kenneth_Hayr "Sir Kenneth Hayr") (66), a New Zealand born former [fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_pilot "Fighter pilot") and retired [air marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_marshal "Air marshal") in the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"). He had been a [Cadet Warrant Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadet_Warrant_Officer "Cadet Warrant Officer") in the [No 3 (City of Auckland) Squadron, Air Training Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Air_Training_Corps "New Zealand Air Training Corps"). He eventually went on to join the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") in the 1950s, rising to senior rank and later serving as the Inspector of RAF Flight Safety in 1976. Hayr was responsible for overseeing the RAF's role in the [re-capture of the Falkland Islands.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War "Falklands War")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-AOASKH-10) On the day of the display Hayr, with a total of 4,398 flying hours (185 of those with the Vampire), would be [pilot-in-command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot-in-command "Pilot-in-command"), sitting in the left seat of the Vampire. Accompanying him was Jonathan Kerr (33),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-YLGVAMP-11) a [safety pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_safety "Aviation safety") who had been allocated to the Vampire by the [Civil Aviation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Aviation_Authority_(United_Kingdom) "Civil Aviation Authority (United Kingdom)") due to the circumstances following the incident with the Venom that morning.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKVAMP-1)

### Bell P-63 Kingcobra

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Bell P-63 Kingcobra")]

The Bell P-63 Kingcobra used in the display of June 3 was assembled in 1944, at the end of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). The aircraft was stationed with the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") under serial number 42-69097.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-AVADKC-4) It was built to conventional standard as a single seat aircraft.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKKC-12) After completing its service in the US Air Force, the Kingcobra was sold under new [civil registration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_registration "Aircraft registration") N52113 in 1947, beginning its career as an [air racer craft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_racing "Air racing"). It remained as a racer for the next four decades, changing hands multiple times but keeping the same registration (N52113), before finally being sold to [Patina Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patina_Ltd&action=edit&redlink=1 "Patina Ltd (page does not exist)") in [Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey "Jersey") with civil registration G-BTWR in 1991.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-AVADKC-4) At this time the Kingcobra was completely rebuilt, with a new [zero-timed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_engine "Aircraft engine") 1,325-horsepower (988 kW) liquid-cooled [Allison V1710-117 piston engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allison_V-1710 "Allison V-1710") located behind the pilot, [gearbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller_speed_reduction_unit "Propeller speed reduction unit") and [propeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller "Propeller").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKKC-12)

[Red Arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Arrows "Red Arrows") pilot and [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") captain Guy Bancroft-Wilson (43)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKKC-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-CLGBWA-13) was flying the Kingcobra on the day of its display,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-ASNKC-3) having began [flight training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_training "Flight training") whilst serving. Bancroft-Wilson finished a three year [tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_duty "Tour of duty") as part of the [Red Arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Arrows "Red Arrows"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-SWABHP-14) flying [Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAE_Systems_Hawk "BAE Systems Hawk") aircraft, continuing to [fly professionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_aviation "Commercial aviation") thereafter. Despite only having 13 hours of flying experience with the Kingcobra, Bancroft-Wilson had accumulated 7,730 hours of flying time overall.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKKC-12) He also held a [display authorisation for a Cat C aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_licensing_and_certification "Pilot licensing and certification") (the Kingcobra being of this category).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKKC-12) This requires the pilot perform a minimum of three display sequence practices in an aircraft of the same category, not preceding 90 days before the day of the public display.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-CAP1724-15) Bancroft-Wilson had flown 30 minutes of dual instruction in a [Texan Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_T-6_Texan "North American T-6 Texan"), 25 minutes of display exercise in the Kingcobra two days before the airshow display and the display itself on June 2. These were not recorded in his [pilot logbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_logbook "Pilot logbook") however, instead being recorded as completed by [Patina Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patina_Ltd&action=edit&redlink=1 "Patina Ltd (page does not exist)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Biggin_Hill_Airshow_disasters#cite_note-GOVUKKC-12)
